title: The Board Resolves
synopsis: Maps the emerging tripartite structure of global power: Musk's vertically integrated energy-compute-finance stack, Google's quietly indispensable Western infrastructure, and China's sovereign parallel civilisation, with orbital access as the unclaimed territory that may decide the age of abundant intelligence.

content:
The trajectories are measurable, and I want to start there, because what follows will sound like speculation and some of it is. The cost curves for AI compute, solar energy and robotics are empirical. They're published quarterly. They move in one direction. Follow them forward a few years with a pencil and some honesty and you arrive at a picture of the world that most people aren't yet willing to look at directly.

I'm going to try to look at it directly. I'll get parts of it wrong. I think the shape is legible, and I think the discomfort we feel trying to describe it comes from how thoroughly it challenges the assumptions we built our lives around rather than from any implausibility.

Start with intelligence, because intelligence is the solvent that dissolves everything else.

Frontier model capabilities are improving at a rate that has, if anything, been accelerating. Benchmarks fall quarterly, context windows expand, reasoning sharpens, cost per token collapses. I won't claim to know the precise moment these systems cross whatever threshold we eventually agree to call general intelligence, because nobody knows that. The curves don't suggest decades. They suggest proximity - perhaps something resembling early AGI by mid 2026, perhaps something that no longer needs the qualifier by late 2027.

I hold that loosely. I hold it.

Once you hold it, even loosely, everything downstream rearranges, because general intelligence dissolves the constraints every other industry and institution was built around. Labour scarcity. Cognitive bottlenecks. The assumption that knowledge work requires human minds. Once those go, the architecture of the world has to be rebuilt, and the question becomes who rebuilds it and on what foundation.

I think the board resolves into three.

**The Vertical Stack**

Consider the last few months. SpaceX absorbed xAI in February, valuing the combined entity around 1.25 trillion dollars, with the IPO confirmed for mid 2026 at a reported target near 1.75 trillion. The stated purpose of the raise, written plainly in federal filings, is orbital data centres: modified Starlink satellites generating and consuming compute in space, powered by uninterrupted solar. The filing language referenced Kardashev Level 2 civilisation. That's federal paperwork, not my editorialising.

Meanwhile Wedbush's Daniel Ives has been saying publicly what the structure has been whispering for a while, that Tesla may follow, and that consolidation is the logical terminus of Musk's architecture. Lay the pieces out and you can see why.

Tesla produces solar panels, battery storage, electric vehicles, autonomous driving software, humanoid robots and AI training chips. SpaceX produces launch infrastructure, satellite internet, and potentially the largest energy generation capacity in history. xAI produces the intelligence layer. These are subsystems of a single vertical stack wearing different corporate clothes, and once unified under one equity structure the compounding begins in earnest.

X Money launched in limited beta this month. Six percent yield on deposits, a Visa partnership, licences in over forty American states, peer to peer transfers and debit cards and direct deposit. Musk's stated ambition is that when something involves money it will happen on this platform, and he's been saying versions of that since X.com in 1999. What's different now is that the platform sits atop an energy and manufacturing stack giving the financial layer something to actually denominate.

I want to be careful. The gap between ambition and execution is real, and Musk has a long history of timelines slipping by years. X Money may fail to reach adoption. The Tesla merger may not happen. The orbital data centres may prove uneconomical. I'm claiming no inevitability. I'm tracing a trajectory, and it points somewhere specific: one interconnected entity controlling energy production, energy storage, physical labour, cognitive labour, compute infrastructure, communications, financial infrastructure and orbital access, simultaneously, under one corporate structure.

The East India Company is the closest historical analogy and even that flatters the past, because the Company operated within the constraints of its era. The entity I'm describing would operate in an era where most of the old constraints have been dissolved by the very intelligence it helped create.

**The Infrastructure You Can't See**

Google requires a different kind of attention, because Google's power doesn't announce itself.

Musk builds things you can photograph. Rockets on landing pads. Robots walking across stages. Google builds things you can't see until you try to remove them, at which point you discover they're load-bearing. The advertising business is the visible revenue, and underneath it runs infrastructure so deeply woven into the daily function of Western economies that extracting it would be roughly as straightforward as extracting the electrical grid. Cloud services hosting a significant share of the internet. Android on three billion devices. The mapping layer logistics and navigation depend on. Gmail handling a quarter of all email globally. And DeepMind, which arguably produced the most important scientific breakthroughs of the last decade, from protein folding to weather prediction to the transformer architecture the entire industry now runs on.

This matters because general intelligence won't arrive into a vacuum. It arrives into existing infrastructure, and the question of who benefits most from abundant intelligence is largely a question of who already holds the pipes to deploy it at civilisational scale. Google does. The talent is there, the data is flowing, and what changes is that the intelligence animating all of it gets dramatically better while every existing dependency deepens.

Western governments will grumble, as they already do, and regulators will posture. You can't regulate away a dependency you spent two decades building. You can slow it, tax it, wrap it in compliance frameworks. Replacing it within the timeframe that matters is impossible, because the replacement would take longer to build than the transformation will take to arrive.

So Google holds the West through the quiet compounding accumulation of indispensability - the way the telephone network held the twentieth century, or the Roman road system held the provinces. You could theoretically build an alternative. You simply wouldn't, because by the time you finished the world would have moved on.

**The Parallel Stack**

China has been preparing for this with a deliberateness Western commentary consistently underestimates, partly because that commentary frames China's current economic difficulties as structural weakness rather than what they more likely represent, which is the turbulence of a managed transition.

The Great Firewall was never merely a censorship apparatus. Viewed structurally, it may be the most effective protectionist policy in the history of digital commerce, because it forced the creation of a parallel technology stack and that stack is now mature. Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent, Huawei, ByteDance - each mirrors a Western counterpart while operating inside an ecosystem with no dependency on American platforms, American cloud infrastructure or American financial rails. When people describe decoupling as a future risk they're describing something China substantially completed years ago.

The energy position reinforces it. China manufactures roughly eighty percent of the world's solar panels and holds dominant positions in the critical minerals the entire transition physically depends on. Domestic oil demand has already peaked. The EV transition is further advanced than in any other major economy. The financial architecture for a post-dollar trading bloc already exists and carries real volume, with CIPS processing trillions of yuan daily and most Shanghai Cooperation Organisation trade now settling in local currencies.

The AI race is misunderstood as a sprint. It's better understood as two civilisations each building sufficient intelligence to run their respective spheres autonomously. China doesn't need to beat Google to general intelligence. China needs a threshold of capability that makes its own infrastructure self-sustaining, and it's closer to that threshold than most Western analysts will admit.

If the petrodollar system keeps weakening - and I've argued elsewhere that the current Gulf war is accelerating exactly that - the bifurcation deepens. The dollar buys less leverage, American tech sanctions lose teeth as Chinese domestic supply chains mature, and the world sorts itself quietly into two digital civilisations sharing a planet and increasingly little else.

**Where the Ground Softens**

Which leaves space, and I have to be honest that this is where the argument moves from extrapolation towards intuition. The logic is coherent, so let me trace it.

Earth is finite in the economic sense as well as the sentimental one. There's a ceiling to terrestrial energy production, a ceiling to terrestrial compute, a ceiling to how many data centres you can build before exhausting land and water and cooling capacity and the patience of host communities. If intelligence becomes the dominant economic input, and intelligence scales with compute, and compute scales with energy, then the binding constraint on growth becomes the binding constraint on energy - and on the surface of this planet that constraint is hard.

Orbit isn't. Solar energy in space is roughly thirteen times more efficient. No atmosphere, no weather, no night if you position the constellation correctly. SpaceX filed with the FCC proposing up to a million orbital data centre satellites, with the stated rationale that within a few years the lowest cost to generate AI compute would be in space.

If that proves even approximately right, then whoever controls orbital access controls the next energy frontier, and whoever controls the next energy frontier occupies a position analogous to the one central banks hold today.

Musk has said repeatedly that his goal is to make humanity multiplanetary. Most people hear aspiration, or eccentricity, the kind of thing billionaires say at conferences while audiences smile politely. I've started hearing a business plan that happens to also be a civilisational project. Starship is the enabling infrastructure for orbital data centres, which fund lunar manufacturing, which funds Mars. Each step requires the previous one, and the first step - cheap reusable heavy lift - already works. SpaceX launches a rocket every two days. Ten thousand Starlink satellites are already up. The infrastructure to claim the territory above the Earth exists today and nobody else is close enough for the gap to matter on the relevant timescale.

Google secures the West through embedded infrastructure. China secures the East through sovereign technology and parallel trade architecture. And the remaining unclaimed territory, the one that may determine who commands the age of abundant intelligence, appears on no terrestrial map.

**What I'm Doing Here**

I should pause and name what I'm doing. I'm constructing a narrative, and narratives are seductive precisely because they compress complexity into coherence while the world remains under no obligation to cooperate. Google could be broken up by regulators with more spine than I'm crediting them with. China's economy could stall in ways that undermine its ambitions rather than catalyse them. Musk's architecture could fracture under its own contradictions, or under the weight of Musk himself, who remains for all his structural genius among the most erratic people on the public stage.

The incentive structures point this way. The capital flows point this way. The physics of energy and compute point this way. And the timeline, which always felt safely distant, has been collapsing. The IPO is months away. X Money launches next month. The Tesla merger is discussed openly by mainstream analysts. AGI benchmarks fall faster than anyone projected five years ago. These have stopped being forecasts and become calendar items.

I think about Arthur when I write things like this, as I always do. He's too young to understand any of it, and part of me envies that - the part remembering what it felt like when the future was a feeling rather than a series of converging data points.

There's another kind of envy too, and I want to be honest about it.

The world Arthur grows up in, if even a fraction of this holds, is the world I dreamed about as a child. I grew up reading science fiction and watching it and drawing it in the margins of schoolbooks. Orbital stations. Intelligent machines. Robots that could build things. Energy too cheap to hoard. Those were fantasies then, separated from reality by what felt like centuries of incremental progress, accessible only through paperbacks with cracked spines read on a carpet in Adelaide while the world outside the window stayed stubbornly mundane.

Arthur won't experience them as fantasies. He'll experience them as Tuesday. As the way things are. As unremarkable.

I find that I'm jealous of him for it, which is a strange thing for a father to admit. I wanted to live in that world and spent decades imagining it, and now it's arriving and I'm old enough to recognise what's happening and young enough to watch my son walk into it as though it were always there. He'll never know the gap between the dreaming and the having. He'll never understand what it felt like to want this future from the far side of impossibility, carrying it around as a private suspicion the world would probably never confirm. He'll simply grow up inside the thing that used to be science fiction and find it ordinary, which may be the greatest gift one generation can hand the next - a world transformed thoroughly enough that the transformation itself goes invisible.

I don't know whether this is the world he inherits. I suspect it might be, and I hold the suspicion loosely, as I hold all of them, because the future has a long history of humiliating anyone who claims to know its face.

The pattern is visible all the same, and it rhymes with patterns I've read about in other contexts. It would be prudent, I think, to pay attention.
